units.title: Divisibility and the Euclidean Algorithm
units.blurb: Divide with remainders, find greatest common divisors quickly, and solve ax + by = c in whole numbers.

units.title: Primes and Factorization
units.blurb: Test for primes, factor uniquely, and use factorizations to count divisors and study how primes are spread out.

units.title: Congruences
units.blurb: Calculate with remainders: modular arithmetic, fast powers, inverses, linear congruences and the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

units.title: Fermat, Euler and Wilson
units.blurb: Tame huge powers with the theorems of Fermat and Euler, count units with φ, and see why passing Fermat's test does not prove a number prime.

units.title: Orders and Primitive Roots
units.blurb: Find how long the powers of a number take to repeat, find primitive roots, and meet discrete logarithms.

units.title: Cryptography
units.blurb: Put modular arithmetic to work in ciphers, key exchange and RSA.

units.title: Quadratic Residues
units.blurb: Decide which numbers are perfect squares mod p, with Euler's criterion and the law of quadratic reciprocity.

units.title: Diophantine Equations and Continued Fractions
units.blurb: Find whole-number solutions of x² + y² = z², sums of two squares and Pell's equation, with continued fractions as the tool.

topics.title: Divisibility
topics.short: a ∣ b means b = ak for some integer k; if a divides b and c, it divides every combination mb + nc.
topics.trouble: Students read a ∣ b as the fraction a/b, or reverse the roles: 3 ∣ 12 is true, but 12 ∣ 3 is false.

topics.title: The Division Algorithm
topics.short: For a positive divisor b, every integer a can be written as a = bq + r with 0 ≤ r < b, even when a is negative.
topics.trouble: Students give a negative remainder for a negative dividend. Since −17 = 5 · (−4) + 3, the remainder is 3, not −2.

topics.title: Writing Numbers in Other Bases
topics.short: Convert to base b by dividing by b again and again, then read the remainders from last to first.
topics.trouble: Students write the remainders in the order they found them, which puts the digits backward.

topics.title: The Euclidean Algorithm
topics.short: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, r), where r is the remainder when a is divided by b; repeat until the remainder is 0.
topics.trouble: Students report the last quotient, or the final remainder 0, instead of the last nonzero remainder.

topics.title: Bézout's Identity and the Extended Euclidean Algorithm
topics.short: Work the Euclidean algorithm backward to write gcd(a, b) = ax + by.
topics.trouble: Students lose track of signs while substituting back. Check that ax + by really equals the gcd.

topics.title: Linear Diophantine Equations
topics.short: ax + by = c has integer solutions exactly when d = gcd(a, b) divides c, and then x = x₀ + (b/d)t, y = y₀ − (a/d)t.
topics.trouble: Students step by b and a instead of b/d and a/d and miss solutions, or forget to scale the Bézout solution by c/d.

topics.title: Testing Primes and the Sieve of Eratosthenes
topics.short: n is prime when no prime up to √n divides it; the sieve crosses out multiples to list every prime up to N.
topics.trouble: Students test divisors all the way up to n, or stop before reaching √n. And 1 is not prime.

topics.title: Unique Prime Factorization
topics.short: Every integer above 1 is a product of primes in exactly one way, because a prime that divides ab divides a or b (Euclid's lemma).
topics.trouble: Students use Euclid's lemma for a divisor that is not prime: 6 ∣ 4 · 9, but 6 divides neither 4 nor 9.

topics.title: gcd and lcm from Prime Factorizations
topics.short: Take the smaller exponent of each prime for the gcd and the larger for the lcm; then gcd(a, b) · lcm(a, b) = ab.
topics.trouble: Students take the larger exponents for the gcd, or expect gcd · lcm to equal the product for three numbers too (for 2, 2 and 2 it gives 4, not 8).

topics.title: Counting and Adding Divisors
topics.short: If n = p₁^a₁ ⋯ pₖ^aₖ, then n has (a₁ + 1)⋯(aₖ + 1) divisors, and their sum σ(n) is a product of geometric sums.
topics.trouble: Students multiply the exponents instead of the exponents plus one, forgetting that each prime can also appear to the power 0.

topics.title: Perfect Numbers and Mersenne Primes
topics.short: n is perfect when σ(n) = 2n; whenever 2ᵖ − 1 is prime, 2ᵖ⁻¹(2ᵖ − 1) is perfect.
topics.trouble: Students think 2ᵖ − 1 is prime whenever p is prime, but 2¹¹ − 1 = 2047 = 23 · 89.

topics.title: Prime Powers in n!
topics.short: The exponent of p in n! is ⌊n/p⌋ + ⌊n/p²⌋ + ⌊n/p³⌋ + ⋯, so 100! ends in 24 zeros.
topics.trouble: Students count only the multiples of 5 and miss that 25, 50, 75 and 100 each bring an extra factor of 5.

topics.title: Infinitely Many Primes
topics.short: Euclid's argument: p₁p₂⋯pₖ + 1 has a prime factor that is not on the list p₁, …, pₖ.
topics.trouble: Students think p₁p₂⋯pₖ + 1 must itself be prime, but 2 · 3 · 5 · 7 · 11 · 13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 · 509.

topics.title: How Common Are Primes?
topics.short: The prime number theorem: there are about x/ln x primes up to x. Primes thin out, and n! + 2, …, n! + n is a run of n − 1 composite numbers.
topics.trouble: Students read x/ln x as the exact count. It is an estimate (78,498 primes are below one million; the estimate gives about 72,382), and its relative error shrinks as x grows.

topics.title: Congruence mod n
topics.short: a ≡ b (mod n) when n ∣ (a − b), that is, when a and b leave the same remainder on division by n.
topics.trouble: Students drop the sign of a negative number and write −3 ≡ 3 (mod 7). In fact −3 ≡ 4 (mod 7).

topics.title: Arithmetic mod n
topics.short: Reduce first, then add, subtract and multiply: the result is the same as reducing at the end.
topics.trouble: Students cancel a common factor from both sides of a congruence: 2 · 3 ≡ 2 · 1 (mod 4), yet 3 ≢ 1 (mod 4).

topics.title: Divisibility Tests from Congruences
topics.short: Since 10 ≡ 1 (mod 9) and 10 ≡ −1 (mod 11), digit sums and alternating digit sums test divisibility by 9 and by 11.
topics.trouble: Students find a remainder mod 11 with the alternating sum started from the leftmost digit. That can give the negative of the true remainder; start with the ones digit.

topics.title: Fast Powers mod n
topics.short: Square again and again, multiply the powers that match the binary digits of the exponent, and reduce after every step.
topics.trouble: Students compute the whole power before reducing, which makes the numbers far too large. Reduce after every multiplication.

topics.title: Modular Inverses
topics.short: a has an inverse mod n exactly when gcd(a, n) = 1; find it with the extended Euclidean algorithm.
topics.trouble: Students expect every nonzero number to have an inverse, but 2 has no inverse mod 6 because gcd(2, 6) = 2: the multiples of 2 mod 6 are only 0, 2 and 4.

topics.title: Linear Congruences
topics.short: ax ≡ b (mod n) has no solution unless d = gcd(a, n) divides b, and then it has exactly d solutions mod n.
topics.trouble: Students give one solution when there are d of them, or divide a and b by d but forget to divide n.

topics.title: The Chinese Remainder Theorem
topics.short: When m and n are coprime, the pair x ≡ a (mod m), x ≡ b (mod n) has exactly one solution mod mn.
topics.trouble: Students use the theorem when the moduli share a factor. Then there may be no solution (x ≡ 1 mod 4 and x ≡ 2 mod 6) or several.

topics.title: Fermat's Little Theorem
topics.short: If p is prime and p ∤ a, then aᵖ⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod p), so exponents can be reduced mod p − 1.
topics.trouble: Students reduce the exponent mod p instead of mod p − 1, or use the theorem when p divides a.

topics.title: Wilson's Theorem
topics.short: An integer p > 1 is prime exactly when (p − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod p): the factors from 2 to p − 2 pair up with their inverses, leaving 1 · (p − 1) ≡ −1.
topics.trouble: Students expect (n − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod n) for every n, but for n = 6, 5! = 120 ≡ 0 (mod 6).

topics.title: Euler's Phi Function
topics.short: φ(n) counts the k from 1 to n with gcd(k, n) = 1; φ(pᵏ) = pᵏ − pᵏ⁻¹, and φ(mn) = φ(m)φ(n) when gcd(m, n) = 1.
topics.trouble: Students multiply φ values for factors that share a prime: φ(4) = 2, not φ(2) · φ(2) = 1.

topics.title: Euler's Theorem
topics.short: If gcd(a, n) = 1, then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n); use it to find the last digits of huge powers.
topics.trouble: Students reduce the exponent mod n instead of mod φ(n), or use the theorem when gcd(a, n) > 1.

topics.title: Fermat Tests and Pseudoprimes
topics.short: If aⁿ⁻¹ ≢ 1 (mod n) for some a with 1 < a < n, then n is composite; passing the test does not prove that n is prime.
topics.trouble: Students treat the converse of Fermat's theorem as true, but 2³⁴⁰ ≡ 1 (mod 341) and 341 = 11 · 31.

topics.title: The Order of an Element
topics.short: The order of a mod n is the smallest k > 0 with aᵏ ≡ 1; it divides φ(n), and the powers of a repeat with that period.
topics.trouble: Students take φ(n) as the order, but the order can be any divisor of φ(n): the order of 2 mod 7 is 3, not 6.

topics.title: Primitive Roots
topics.short: g is a primitive root mod p when its order is p − 1, so its powers reach every nonzero residue; check that g^((p − 1)/q) ≢ 1 for each prime q dividing p − 1.
topics.trouble: Students check only that g^(p − 1) ≡ 1, which every nonzero g passes by Fermat's theorem.

topics.title: Discrete Logarithms
topics.short: With a primitive root g mod p, every nonzero residue is gᵏ for exactly one k mod p − 1; checking a k is easy, finding one is slow.
topics.trouble: Students reduce the discrete logarithm mod p instead of mod p − 1.

topics.title: Shift and Affine Ciphers
topics.short: Encrypt letters with x ↦ ax + b (mod 26) and decrypt with x ↦ a⁻¹(x − b); a must be coprime to 26.
topics.trouble: Students decrypt by subtracting b and dividing by a as ordinary numbers instead of multiplying by the inverse of a mod 26.

topics.title: Diffie–Hellman Key Exchange
topics.short: Two people agree on a secret g^(ab) mod p while sharing only gᵃ and gᵇ in public.
topics.trouble: Students compute the shared key as gᵃ · gᵇ = g^(a + b) instead of (gᵃ)ᵇ = g^(ab).

topics.title: The RSA Cryptosystem
topics.short: The public key is (n, e) with n = pq; the private key d ≡ e⁻¹ (mod φ(n)); encrypt with c ≡ mᵉ and decrypt with m ≡ cᵈ (mod n).
topics.trouble: Students find d as the inverse of e mod n instead of mod φ(n) = (p − 1)(q − 1).

topics.title: Squares mod p
topics.short: a is a quadratic residue mod p when x² ≡ a has a solution; for an odd prime p, exactly half of the nonzero residues are squares.
topics.trouble: Students forget that x and −x have the same square, and expect p − 1 different nonzero squares.

topics.title: The Legendre Symbol and Euler's Criterion
topics.short: For p ∤ a, (a/p) is 1 when a is a square mod p and −1 when it is not, and (a/p) ≡ a^((p − 1)/2) (mod p).
topics.trouble: Students read the Legendre symbol (a/p) as the fraction a ÷ p.

topics.title: Is −1 or 2 a Square mod p?
topics.short: −1 is a square mod an odd prime p exactly when p ≡ 1 (mod 4), and 2 is a square exactly when p ≡ ±1 (mod 8).
topics.trouble: Students use the rule for −1 on 2, or look at p mod 4 when the rule for 2 needs p mod 8.

topics.title: Quadratic Reciprocity
topics.short: For odd primes p ≠ q, (p/q) = (q/p), except when p ≡ q ≡ 3 (mod 4), when (p/q) = −(q/p).
topics.trouble: Students flip a symbol whose top number is not an odd prime (factor it first), or forget the minus sign when both primes are 3 mod 4.

topics.title: Pythagorean Triples
topics.short: Every primitive triple is (m² − n², 2mn, m² + n²), up to the order of the legs, with m > n > 0, m and n coprime and of opposite parity.
topics.trouble: Students use an m and n that are both odd or share a factor, and get a triple that is not primitive: m = 3, n = 1 gives (8, 6, 10).

topics.title: Sums of Two Squares
topics.short: n is a sum of two squares exactly when every prime ≡ 3 (mod 4) appears in its factorization to an even power.
topics.trouble: Students rule out every n with a prime factor that is 3 mod 4, but 45 = 3² · 5 = 6² + 3².

topics.title: Continued Fractions of Rational Numbers
topics.short: The quotients of the Euclidean algorithm give a/b = [q₀; q₁, q₂, …], and the convergents are better and better approximations.
topics.trouble: Students drop the whole-number part q₀, or rebuild the fraction from the outside in instead of from the innermost term out.

topics.title: Continued Fractions of Square Roots
topics.short: When d is not a perfect square, √d has a repeating continued fraction, and its convergents are the best rational approximations: no fraction with a smaller denominator comes closer.
topics.trouble: Students switch to rounded decimals, which hides the repeating pattern. Keep exact expressions such as 1/(√7 − 2) and rationalize.

topics.title: Pell's Equation
topics.short: For d > 0 not a perfect square, x² − dy² = 1 has a smallest solution with y > 0, found among the convergents of √d, and the powers of x₁ + y₁√d give all the others.
topics.trouble: Students offer x = 1, y = 0 as the fundamental solution. It is the trivial one; the fundamental solution is the smallest with y > 0.
